title: Deaf Graduate's AI Alarm SIVO.GO Wins UK James Dyson Award and £5,000
excerpt: Gargi Agrawalla, 23, built SIVO.GO from her own experience of missing alarms with her cochlear implant off; it turns fire alarms and doorbells into light and vibration.
body:
• Gargi Agrawalla, a 23-year-old Loughborough University product design graduate born profoundly deaf, built SIVO.GO, an AI device that alerts deaf users to fire alarms, doorbells and knocks.
  • The device runs its AI on the unit itself — trained on more than 500 sound samples, with no Wi-Fi or cloud processing — and answers with colour-coded lights, screen symbols and vibrations.
  • SIVO.GO won the UK James Dyson Award and a £5,000 prize fund to improve reliability, expand user trials and work toward certification and pilot manufacture.
  • It is still a prototype and is not on sale; the award's 2026 global winners were Sentinel from the Philippines and Rumble Rims from Harvard, £30,000 each.

For a deaf traveller in an unfamiliar hotel room, the dangerous hours are the ones with the hearing technology off — asleep, or in the shower, when a fire alarm or a knock at the door can go unnoticed. Gargi Agrawalla, a 23-year-old product design graduate of Loughborough University who was born profoundly deaf, built her final-year project around exactly that gap. The result, SIVO.GO, has won the UK James Dyson Award, Dezeen reported.

"SIVO.GO came from my own experience as a deaf cochlear implant user and the anxiety I felt when travelling or staying somewhere unfamiliar."

— Gargi Agrawalla, designer of SIVO.GO

Agrawalla received a cochlear implant at age 12, which allowed her to hear sounds for the first time. But the implant's external sound processor has to be removed for sleeping and showering, and she found that emergency alarms, doorbells and room signals in hotels are, as the BBC reported her experience, "not always visual, tactile or accessible." Existing alarms for deaf and hard-of-hearing people tend to be bulky, expensive and built for a single sound — a fire alarm, or a crying baby — so a traveller ends up packing several devices.

How it works

SIVO.GO uses an AI model trained on more than 500 sound samples to distinguish between noises, from doorbells to alarms. The model runs locally on the device rather than through Wi-Fi or the cloud, which Agrawalla says preserves privacy and keeps it working without an internet connection; The Times reported the prototype connects by Bluetooth. Alerts are delivered through colour-coded lights, screen symbols and haptic vibrations. The device is portable — carried on a lanyard or in a pocket, mounted on a bathroom wall, where it flashes red for an alarm, or placed under a pillow as a vibrating alarm clock, according to The Times.

Knocking proved the hardest sound. In testing, the AI confused knocks with footsteps or tapping on a table, even after more training samples were added. Her fix was a separate, optional vibration sensor that mounts discreetly behind a door to detect knocking or forced entry directly.

What the award changes

As the UK winner, Agrawalla receives a £5,000 prize fund to support the next stages of development: improving reliability, expanding trials with deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and working towards certification and pilot manufacture, according to Dezeen. Rumyana Dancheva, a Dyson lead design engineer on the UK judging panel, called the device "a brilliant example of a simple solution to a complex problem," the BBC reported.

Agrawalla has also said the same alert system could help people with tinnitus, neurodiverse users, new parents and older users. At the award's international stage, SIVO.GO was not among the global winners: the 2026 global prizes of £30,000 each went to Sentinel, a Philippine building-damage sensor, and Rumble Rims, a concussion headset developed at Harvard University, according to The Times of India. SIVO.GO remains a prototype — the £5,000 is development money, not a product launch — but it is now a funded one, with trials and certification as the stated next steps.
image_caption: Gargi Agrawalla holds the components of SIVO.GO, the AI alert device she designed as her final-year project at Loughborough University. The device won the UK James Dyson Award, carrying a £5,000 prize fund for its next stage of development.
nri_angle: An Indian-origin designer in the UK turned her own experience of deafness into an award-winning safety device — the kind of diaspora engineering story that starts in a dorm room and aims at every hotel room.
author: Diaspora Desk
